items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' or ran any warm-up. The customer opened with 'Garrison. I am, I need to schedule a move' — a buying signal delivered by name — and got 'Okay. Yeah, well, I can certainly help you out with that. First things first. Do you happen to have a date in mind?'

No 'sound good?' confirmation on the agenda. He gave a real roadmap — 'let me go ahead and plug in some contact info and then I'll ask you a whole bunch of questions about the move' — and then never paused for the customer to agree to it, and never gave a timeframe. On a call that ran 12.7 minutes, telling the customer up front how long it would take was worth doing.
Additional rooms never probed — no storage closet, no patio, no balcony, no shared storage cage. Both units are apartments and neither was asked about.

Packing needs never asked. The customer said his clothes and kitchen items 'are going into boxes' — future tense, not yet packed — and Garrison never asked whether he wanted help packing them, never offered the service, and never quoted it.

Moving-stressor question never asked. The customer volunteered it himself anyway ('the hardest part about this move is going down to two flex of stairs'), which Garrison acknowledged warmly, but the question that surfaces the concerns a customer will not volunteer was never put.
Packing service pricing never given, on a customer with unpacked boxes and a stated willingness to spend more.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned — 12.7 minutes, a full pricing walkthrough, and not one word about the $2,000, the repair/replace/reimburse mechanism, the brand name, or the 60-cents-per-pound baseline. The customer is carrying a wall-mounted TV and a full-size dresser down two flights of stairs and heard nothing about what happens if we drop either one.
Packing time never factored into the estimate, on boxes that do not yet exist.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used to make two-and-a-half-to-three-and-a-half hours concrete.

Zero booking attempt — the single most costly miss on the call. The customer's first sentence was 'I need to schedule a move,' Garrison confirmed availability on the date in his second sentence ('we absolutely do have availability on that date'), and then never once asked for it. The close was entirely passive: 'if you'd like to move forward with us, it is completely free and very simple. All you have to do is just give us a call or you can respond directly to that email.'

He actively routed the customer to competitors: 'at the very least you know, you can utilize that information that I send you here to kind of compare and contrast with some of those other companies out there.' That is a self-inflicted loss — a customer who called in ready to book was handed a shopping assignment.

BOLDED-details framing absent, and the 'reply with any corrections' verification ask absent. He asked the customer to reply to book, not to reply to verify — and he took down two unit numbers, two square footages, an inventory list and a wall-mounted TV entirely by ear with no read-back.
Hours and how to reach us never given.
Save Your Ass entirely absent — 0/10. See the coaching note; this was the strongest setup for it in the whole batch.
Customer's name never used once. He collected 'Scott brown' at the thirty-second mark and never said it again across twelve more minutes.
top_strength: Garrison's probing on access is the best technical work in this batch, and it is the reason his estimate is also the most honest one this week. He did not accept the first answer on the walk distance — he asked three times, in escalating specificity, until he had a number he could actually use: 'how far of a walk would you say it might be from unit two? Unit,' then 'all in, all between that kind of like, that entire walk there if you could put it in feet, how far do you think that might be?' and the customer finally produced '1215 feet maybe.' Most reps in this sample take 'not that far' and move on. He also mapped the route rather than the distance — the customer narrated the full path ('come down two flights of stairs out the building doors across a street that doesn't allow cars on it... into the building down the hallway and up an elevator') and Garrison drew the right operational conclusion out loud: 'Sounds like we won't even really need to load up the truck. Yeah, we'll just be able to walk everything, right? From unit to unit.' Then he did the thing the estimate-accuracy rock is actually asking for. He stated the benchmark, then moved off it in the direction the evidence pointed — downward: 'what we usually see in a home of, of the size and scale. Is it something on average we see take, takes two movers somewhere between two and a half to three and a half hours to complete. I think based on everything we've talked about here we will absolutely fall within that range potentially even on the lower end of it. Because of course, we don't even have to worry about loading up a truck. So I would think if anything, this will probably come in a lot closer to the two and a half to three hour range.' Benchmark, job-specific adjustment, stated reason, and a range that tightens rather than widens. He is one of only two reps this week to shade a quote down based on access facts, and he immediately backed it with the protection the customer needs to accept it: 'keep in mind that's just an estimate we're only gonna bill you for the actual time. We use.' His Clock section is a clean 4/4 — the only perfect clock in the batch besides Nicole's — covering the on-site start, the make-contact trigger, the 2.5-hour minimum, the fifteen-minute proration, and a sense-check that got a real answer: 'does that all make sense so far.' 'It does.' And the honesty on the TV mount was the right call commercially even though it cost him: he did not fudge it, he explained exactly why ('our movers are not trained on installing anything into the walls. We don't have stud finders'), and he drew the line precisely — we can take it off, we can hang it on an existing mount, we cannot install the mount.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, and it is not subtle: a customer opened this call with 'I need to schedule a move,' named a date, confirmed availability in the first thirty seconds, gave twelve minutes of cooperative detail, and Garrison never asked for the booking. Not once. The close was 'if you'd like to move forward with us... just give us a call or you can respond directly to that email,' and then he went further and told the customer to go shop us: 'you can utilize that information that I send you here to kind of compare and contrast with some of those other companies out there.' That line is generous and it is costing him money. He had every reason to close — availability confirmed, no deposit, a move on October 9th that is three weeks out. What he needed at the TV-mount moment was to keep the date rather than release the customer: 'Totally fair, and I'd want it done in one go too. Here's what I'd suggest — there's no deposit and no card on file, so let me hold Friday the ninth for you right now. It costs you nothing, you keep the date while you make those calls, and if you find someone who can do the mount you just let me know and I'll release it.' That converts the objection into a hold instead of a goodbye. Rule to install: if the customer said the words 'schedule' or 'book' at any point, you ask for the date before you hang up. Second priority, and this is the one that would have solved his actual problem: Save Your Ass is a zero on the best Save-Your-Ass setup in this entire week's sample. The customer said, in plain English, 'I don't mind paying a little more to make sure it gets done faster so we come in right at the two and a half hours.' That is a customer explicitly asking how to make the move shorter. Garrison's answer was that he could not add movers. The real answer was sitting right there: 'Here's the better version of that, and it's free. You're moving across a walkway, not across town — so anything you can carry, carry. Loose stuff in the drawers, the closet odds and ends, the pictures off the walls, the small kitchen items. Every trip you make before Friday comes straight off the clock, and on a move this short that is what actually holds you at the two and a half. Does that make sense?' That answers his question better than a third mover would have, and it is the single highest-value thirty seconds available on this call. Third, the differentiators. No Worries, Meet Your Mover and On-Time Guarantee are all absent from a 12.7-minute call — which means he had the time and spent it elsewhere. Note the specific cost of the No Worries omission here: the customer is watching a dresser, a full bed and a wall-mounted TV go down two flights of stairs, said the stairs were his biggest worry, and never heard that we set aside $2,000 per move. On estimate accuracy, no flag — this one is a positive data point. He quoted 2.5 to 3 hours against a stated benchmark of 2.5 to 3.5, and justified going low with a real access fact (no truck loading). That is exactly the behavior the bottom-4 work is trying to produce; the reason it did not convert is the close, not the number. Worth using this call as the positive counterexample in a calibration session — same rubric, same week, and his estimate discipline is the opposite of the padding pattern. Last, efficiency: 12.7 minutes without the differentiators or the prep speech means the time went into filler. 'Perfect, perfect,' 'Gotcha, gotcha,' 'absolutely, without a doubt, without a doubt' — that is roughly a minute of runway he could spend on the three differentiators and the carload tip instead.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and affirming, and genuinely responsive rather than scripted — he acknowledged the customer's reasoning instead of plowing past it ('I see. Okay, that makes Perfect Sense'), validated the stairs concern rather than minimizing it ('That's definitely gonna be the tough this part absolutely... it certainly will slow us down a little bit'), and handled the TV-mount limitation with no defensiveness at all; held off a 5 by never once using the customer's name across 12.7 minutes and by leaning hard on doubled filler affirmations — 'Perfect, perfect,' 'Gotcha, gotcha,' 'without a doubt, without a doubt' — that start to read as reflex rather than response.
audio_review_reason: The efficiency bullet was deducted on transcript evidence alone, and that evidence is ambiguous. The transcript shows a very high density of doubled affirmations ('Perfect, perfect,' 'Gotcha, gotcha, and all in, all between,' 'Absolutely. Okay, fantastic') and several sentences that restart mid-clause. From text there is no way to tell whether Garrison sounds warm and engaged with a verbal tic, or whether he sounds like he is filling airtime while typing — and the distinction changes the coaching entirely. It is also worth hearing the close: on paper 'you can compare and contrast with some of those other companies out there' reads as a rep giving the sale away, and the audio would confirm whether that was said as genuine service confidence or as resignation after the TV-mount objection.
